newsitem.title: USA: Clinton likely to recover fully, return to jogging.
newsitem.headline: Clinton likely to recover fully, return to jogging.

text.p: President Bill Clinton should make a full recovery from his knee injury within a few months and return to his role as the nation's First Jogger, orthopedic surgeons said on Friday.
"If he was a professional athlete, this wouldn't be a career-ender, although it could be a season-ender," said Dr. Donald Rose, an orthopedic surgeon at New York's Hospital for Joint Diseases.

Orthopedic surgeons and sports medicine experts said there was a very good chance that Clinton would feel well enough to attend the scheduled summit in Helsinki with Russian President Boris Yeltsin next week, although he would be on crutches.

"Certainly, the way he travels, I would think he would be able to go," said Dr. Stephen Haas, a Washington orthopedist who operated on Vice President Al Gore when he ripped his Achilles' tendon on a basketball court in 1994.
Doctors said by early next week, Clinton should not need prescription-strength painkillers, though he might need some mild over-the-counter ones.

Clinton tore a tendon in his right knee early on Friday morning in Florida, and was to undergo repair surgery Friday afternoon at the National Naval Medical Centre in Bethesda, Maryland. All doctors interviewed described it as a routine surgical procedure.

Although recovery patterns vary, doctors said that a healthy middle-aged male like Clinton with a torn knee tendon would probably be walking on crutches in a day or two, stay on crutches for about six weeks, and be back to all normal activities including jogging and sports in four to six months.
Clinton's knee will be immobilized in a brace, or possibly a cast, and he will need a few months of physical therapy to restore flexibility and strength.

The doctors said surgery to repair a torn quadriceps tendon was straightforward. The procedure lasts about an hour, during which the surgeons repair the tendon, a piece of connective tissue that attaches the large quad muscle in the front of the thigh to the knee.

Clinton will not need general anaesthetic, so presidential power does not have to be transferred temporarily to Gore. He will instead have an epidural, an anaesthetic that blocks pain in the lower half of the body.
Patients usually stay in the hospital overnight, although the some patients go home the same day they have the surgery.

According to the American Academy of Orthopedic Surgeons, there were 7,000 hospital admissions for this injury in 1994, the most recent data available. Knee injuries involving ligaments and cartilage are more common.
Surgeons say they see this injury in professional athletes, but it is also relatively common in middle-aged men.
